title: Open-plan office noise: Cognitive performance and restoration
research_question: 1. How do two levels of open-plan office noise (high vs. low) affect cognitive performance, emotional self-ratings, and physiological stress during work? 2. How do varying sound conditions (nature movie+sound, river sound only, silence, office noise) during a short restoration period affect recovery from fatigue and stress after work?

participants.description: 47 students (27 female; mean age = 26) from the University of Gävle. 9 participants excluded from analysis due to failures to follow task instructions or equipment malfunctioning, leaving 38 for analysis.
participants.recruitment: Recruited from the University of Gävle, compensated with 990 Swedish crowns.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Simulated open-plan office noise conditions. High noise: 51 dBA LAeq (recorded office noise + phone/speech signals). Low noise: 39 dBA LAeq (high noise reduced by 12 dB).
Nature movie with river sounds: Film clips of streaming water in different landscapes with corresponding binaural river sounds.
River sound only: Binaural river sounds without film clips.
Office noise: Continuing to listen to the high office noise (51 dBA LAeq) from the work period.

measures.instrument: PI-points (sum of words recalled from correct list)
PI-no answers (sum of words not remembered)
Operation Span (correct math operations + words remembered)
Short texts with multiple-choice questions (sum of correct answers)
Updating task (recall 3 smallest numbers in order)
High Performance Liquid Chromatography (HPLC) of urine samples

findings.antecedent: High office noise (51 LAeq) vs. Low office noise (39 LAeq) during work (first session)
findings.mechanism: Noise impairs working memory processes, leading to fewer words remembered.
findings.source: 3.1. Noise effects on cognitive performance, p.6
findings.quote: a significant main effect of noise on memory for words (PI-points), F (1, 30) = 4.27, p < .05, partial n² = 0.13, indicating a better performance

findings.antecedent: High office noise (51 LAeq) vs. Low office noise (39 LAeq) during work (first session)
findings.mechanism: Noise impairs working memory processes, leading to more forgotten words.
findings.source: 3.1. Noise effects on cognitive performance, p.6
findings.quote: a significant effect of noise on the number of missing answers (PI-no answers), F (1, 30) = 6.62, p < .05, partial ŋ² = 0.18.

findings.antecedent: High office noise (51 LAeq) vs. Low office noise (39 LAeq) during work (first session)
findings.consequent: Other cognitive measures (e.g., response inhibition, logical problems, operation span, reading span, serial recall, shifting, updating)
findings.mechanism: Null finding, possibly due to task type or exposure duration.
findings.source: 3.1. Noise effects on cognitive performance, p.6
findings.quote: There were, however, no statistically significant effects of noise on the other cognitive measures (all Fs < 1).

findings.antecedent: Time (from arrival to after 2h of work)
findings.source: 3.2. Noise effects on acute psychophysiological stress, p.6
findings.quote: an effect of time on the cortisol levels F (1.16, 34.91) = 31.12, p < .001, partial n² = 0.51 (see Fig. 4). The participants showed high levels of cortisol when they arrived to the experimental session, and the level had declined in both noise conditions after 2 h of work.

findings.antecedent: High office noise (51 LAeq) vs. Low office noise (39 LAeq) during work
findings.mechanism: Short-term noise exposure did not significantly alter the natural cortisol decline.
findings.source: 3.2. Noise effects on acute psychophysiological stress, p.6
findings.quote: There was no statistically significant effect of noise on the decline in the level of cortisol (F < 1).

findings.source: 3.2. Noise effects on acute psychophysiological stress, p.6
findings.quote: A significant effect of time was also shown on the norepinephrine levels from the urine samples, F (1, 35) = 30.40, p < 0.001, partial n² = 0.47

findings.antecedent: High office noise (51 LAeq) vs. Low office noise (39 LAeq) during work
findings.mechanism: Short-term noise exposure did not significantly affect catecholamine levels.
findings.source: 3.2. Noise effects on acute psychophysiological stress, p.6
findings.quote: There were no statistically significant effects of noise on the level of catecholamines (F < 1).

findings.antecedent: High office noise (51 LAeq) vs. Low office noise (39 LAeq) during work * Time (Pretest to Postwork)
findings.mechanism: High noise increases cognitive load and effort, leading to greater self-reported fatigue over time.
findings.source: 3.3. Noise effects on self ratings of fatigue, p.7
findings.quote: a significant interaction between noise and time on tiredness (yawning), F (2, 32) = 6.25, p < 0.01, partial ŋ² = 0.28

findings.antecedent: High office noise (51 LAeq) vs. Low office noise (39 LAeq) during work * Time (Pretest to Postwork)
findings.mechanism: High noise increases cognitive load and effort, leading to greater self-reported lack of motivation over time.
findings.source: 3.3. Noise effects on self ratings of fatigue, p.7
findings.quote: and on lack of motivation (passiveness) F (2, 32) = 4.33, p < 0.05, partial ŋ² = 0.21.

findings.antecedent: Restoration condition (Nature movie+sound, River sound only, Silence, Office noise)
findings.consequent: Change in self-reported lack of energy (exhaustion)
findings.mechanism: Different environmental conditions during restoration differentially affect perceived energy levels.
findings.quote: a significant between-subjects effect of restorative conditions on change in the ratings of lack of energy (exhaustion), F (3, 29) = 3.10, p < 0.05, partial ŋ² = 0.24

findings.antecedent: Restoration condition (Nature movie+sound, River sound only, Silence, Office noise)
findings.consequent: Change in self-reported lack of motivation (uninterested)
findings.mechanism: Different environmental conditions during restoration differentially affect perceived motivation levels.
findings.quote: and of lack of motivation (uninterested) F (3, 29) = 3.02, p < 0.05, partial n² = 0.24.

findings.antecedent: Nature movie with river sounds vs. Listening to office noise OR Listening to river sounds (during restoration)
findings.mechanism: Multi-sensory nature exposure provides greater restorative benefits than single-sensory or negative stimuli.
findings.quote: the participants who saw the movie (including river sounds) rated themselves as having more energy (i.e., were less exhausted) in comparison with the participants listening to noise (p < 0.01) and those listening to river sounds (p < 0.05).

findings.antecedent: Listening to office noise during restoration vs. Listening to river sounds OR Seeing nature movie
findings.mechanism: Remaining in aversive office noise prevents restoration of motivation, while nature stimuli promote it.
findings.quote: The participants who listened to noise during the restoration period rated themselves as being less motivated (i.e., more uninterested) in comparison with the participants who listened to river sounds (p < 0.05) or saw the movie (p < 0.01)

findings.antecedent: Nature movie with river sounds vs. Listening to office noise OR Listening to river sounds (during restoration)
findings.mechanism: Multi-sensory nature exposure provides greater restorative benefits for perceived tiredness.
findings.quote: The post hoc analysis also demonstrated a marginal difference in tiredness (yawning) between the movie condition and the noise condition (p = 0.055) and between the movie and river sound conditions (p = 0.052).

findings.antecedent: Restoration condition (Nature movie+sound, River sound only, Silence, Office noise)
findings.consequent: Cognitive performance OR Physiological measures (cortisol, catecholamines)
findings.mechanism: The 7-minute restoration period was too short to show effects on objective cognitive or physiological measures.
findings.quote: No statistically significant effects from the restoration period were detected on the cognitive or physiological measures.

mechanisms: Noise increases cognitive load and effort, impairing working memory and leading to self-reported fatigue and reduced motivation.
Multi-sensory nature exposure (movie + sound) provides greater restorative benefits for perceived energy and motivation compared to single-sensory (sound only) or aversive (office noise) stimuli.
moderators: Sequence of noise conditions (for cognitive measures)
implementation_implications: Significant reduction of noise level in open-plan offices can reduce negative effects on memory, tiredness, and motivation.
Achieving noise reduction requires simultaneous consideration of noise control measures and silent behavior (office etiquette).
Rest in office noise negatively affects motivation.
A short (7 min) nature movie with corresponding water sound can increase perceived energy more than staying in continued office noise or just listening to river sounds.
Workplaces and urban areas with high noise levels demand compensatory strategies, including access to restorative environments.

tables.description: Analysis of two noise conditions (high noise: 51 dBA, low noise: 39 dBA) in respect with Speech Transmission Index (STI) and time variation.
key_stats: Range of STI values: 0.00 to 0.66 (high noise), 0.00 to 0.58 (low noise)
Overall variation of SPL, LA,eq, 1s dB: 40-60 (high noise), 31-50 (low noise)

tables.description: Mean change in SOFI-measures in different restorative conditions (negative values indicate improvement).

limitations: Small sample size for comparison in each restorative condition.
Brief (7-minute) restoration period may have been too short to show effects on objective cognitive or physiological measures.
Exposure times might have been too short (2 hours) for performance effects to fully appear, as participants might compensate for adverse conditions by exerting extra effort.
Participants' awareness of session duration might have mitigated their tolerance of noise exposure.
Lack of effects on other cognitive measures might be due to the intelligibility of speech (STI) being similar between high and low noise conditions, rather than just overall noise level.

No reliable noise effects on physiological measures suggest that short-term noise effects on cognitive performance are not mediated by physiological changes, but long-term chronic exposure might differ.
The initial 15-minute relaxation period was not sufficient to deal with high stress levels from the start of the experiment.
